newsitem.title: CHINA: US-China tussle may hit Radio Free Asia HK bureau.
newsitem.headline: US-China tussle may hit Radio Free Asia HK bureau.

text.p: Now that Hong Kong is part of China, Radio Free Asia's news bureau here could be an early casualty of an ongoing ideological battle between Washington and Beijing, political and media analysts said on Friday.
"The (mainland) Chinese clearly don't like Radio Free Asia and they've said so but whether that will mean a crackdown is difficult to predict," said one Western political analyst.
"If they were closed down it would generate very negative publicity (for Beijing). It would be a bad sign."
Headquartered in Washington, Radio Free Asia (RFA) is modelled loosely after U.S.-government funded Radio Free Europe, which reached behind the Iron Curtain with broadcasts during the Cold War.

RFA began broadcasting in 1996 on a modest budget of $9.3 million. The operation currently reaches China, including Tibet, five hours a day, as well as Burma, Vietnam and Korea and hopes to reach Laos and Cambodia later this year.

Championed by Washington -- especially by conservative Republicans -- as a voice for democratic values, RFA has been excoriated by some authoritarian Asian rulers, including Beijing, as an outlet for American propaganda.
China successfully pressured several countries into denying RFA a right to locate transmitters on their territory.
While Hong Kong was noted for press freedom under British colonial rule, which ended at midnight on June 30, media here face an uncertain future now the territory has reverted to China.
No outlet is more vulnerable than Radio Free Asia's bureau of three reporters, who see themselves in a frontline of a hard-fought war of words and ideas.
"We are hoping for the best but preparing for the worst," said one RFA staffer in Hong Kong.
"We haven't received any signal yet but we're probably a good test on press freedom for the Hong Kong government. All we can do is keep our heads down and continue reporting."
Radio Free Asia moved centre-stage in relations between Beijing and Washington last month when its funding and broadcast reach were targeted for increase by the U.S. Congress.
The move was sold as an alternative to eliminating China's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status.
RFA insists that it broadcasts only objective news and -- unlike Radio Free Europe or Voice of America -- no editorials.
But the explicit MFN tradeoff has highlighted RFA's role as an instrument of U.S. foreign policy in the minds of Chinese officials.
U.S. government funding makes RFA a logical target for restrictions or perhaps expulsion from Hong Kong once the new government settles into its job, media analysts say.
Many argue that such a move would be more a test of wills between Beijing and Washington than of press freedom.

"If you classify them (RFA) as a U.S. government operation then it would not be a test case for press freedom in the normal sense," said Joseph Man Can, Chairman of Hong Kong's Chinese University department of journalism.
"I think it is difficult to argue that they are not an extension of the U.S. government. I think they would not be a good test case."
Radio Free Asia's managers in Washington say RFA is a likely item on Beijing's action agenda in Hong Kong but make no prediction about what China will do.
"If they shut us down there would be a broad reaction," said Daniel Southerland, RFA's progamming director. "We have wide support in the Congress, not just among conservatives."
